extracted.intended_audience: university students, academics, theologians, and scientifically-minded clergy
extracted.subtask_description: A university lecture discussing the proper relations and boundaries between Theology (Christianity) and the various sciences, and the role of a University in adjudicating and accommodating different branches of knowledge. Emphasises methodological limits, prudence in handling apparent conflicts, and the proper subordinate role of empirical or historical enquiries to theological tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Baconian/empirical method in Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: The Baconian method (Experiment and Induction) is 'mismatched' with Theology and cannot determine theological truth; its arrogant intrusion into sacred territory leads to breakdowns and may produce scepticism or the claim that 'religion is not a science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the empirical/deductive methods meant for natural science as the sole or decisive method for theological questions; recognise the method's legitimate province and avoid using it to dispossess traditional theological method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute Scriptural, Historical, or Physical Religion for Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Religions drawn solely from Scripture, antiquity (Patristic/Historical), or from physical phenomena give only partial truths—probabilities or isolated true items—and are not the whole of Theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scriptural, historical, or physical findings as subordinate, illustrative, or inductive aids to Theology, not as complete replacements; beware of setting any one of these up 'as something complete in itself' against theological tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and scope of Physical (Natural) Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Theology uses phenomena and laws of the material universe to argue design and thereby a Creator; it exhibits prominently three elementary divine notions—Power, Wisdom, and Goodness—but says little or nothing about sanctity, omniscience, justice, mercy, or particular providence, and tells nothing properly Christian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the contributions of Natural Theology (comfort, illustration of some divine attributes) but recognise its intrinsic limits—it cannot speak to the evangelical essentials, miracles, conscience, duty, or the four last things (death, judgment, heaven, hell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of isolated Physical Theology (anti-Christian drift)
rubrics_metrics.description: When separated from supernatural teaching, Physical Theology may lead to a naturalistic or pantheistic religion: a God conceived only by laws can become an idol and may dispose minds against Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow Physical Theology to stand alone; integrate it with theological/supernatural teachings to avoid deforming the idea of God into mere immanence or lawfulness that excludes miracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper subordinate relation of Physical Theology to Theology proper
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'grafted' onto Theology, Physical Theology is in its right place and can illustrate divine omnipotence, prove the miraculousness of Revelation more vividly, and subserve theological truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical arguments as supportive and illustrative material within a theological framework, not as independent or authoritative theological systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: University's mission: admit all departments and assign just boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A University should teach all departments, assign each study its proper place and just boundaries, define mutual relations, repress aggression or encroachment, and convert mutual differences into common good; it acts as 'umpire between truth and truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise and defend the rights and privileges of different disciplines, promote intercommunication, and prevent any one field from usurping another's province by sagacity, wisdom, and forbearance rather than rigid written rules alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method of the university: discrimination over simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: The university philosopher 'defines, rather than analyzes,' recognizes separate truths, accepts the impossibility of fusing all knowledge into one formula, and practices patience and cautious discrimination when facing apparent contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a method that maps distinctions and limits of knowledge, is familiar with signs of real vs. apparent difficulty, and resists reducing complex multiform truth to single formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinal maxims for the university philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: Three guiding precepts: (1) truth cannot be contrary to truth; (2) truth often seems contrary to truth; (3) be patient with such appearances and avoid hasty judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these maxims when adjudicating disputes between disciplines; cultivate patience and equanimity rather than precipitous resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling apparent conflicts between Revelation and Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When science appears to contradict dogma, the Catholic believer should expect one of three outcomes: the scientific point will turn out not to be proved; or not contradictory; or not really part of Revelation (confused with revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond with reasoned reflection, sober judgment, and patience; avoid forcing immediate, possibly mistaken resolutions—'give error rope enough' and rely on Time and reason as interpreters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude of Catholics to scientific discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholics may accept scientific enquiry and results without fear; absolute faith in Revelation does not imply fear of scientific research or hasty suppression of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage scientific research within its proper bounds; trust that genuine science will ultimately be consistent with revealed truth or will be shown fallible in its claims that appear contradictory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings against making partial inquiries into full theological questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many investigations only lead 'a certain way' (to probability, not certainty, or to some true particulars rather than the whole); erecting such limited inquiries into complete sciences misleads—'Half of the truth is a falsehood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat partial, inchoate, or subordinate processes as such; do not elevate them to substitute authoritative teachings on matters of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: Church's moderation and allowance of philosophical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the Church has often allowed philosophical and scientific speculation (e.g., medieval universities, scholasticism, episode of St. Virgilius and Antipodes) and has preferred argument over suppression when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples to justify a temperate policy toward scientific freedom in universities: allow inquiry, moderate disputes by argument and scholarship rather than force or proscription.
